processing: Gongfu black tea: withered, rolled, fully oxidised and dried in the usual way for the class.
harvest_season: Not well documented for this tea; as with other Chinese gongfu blacks, spring leaf makes the finest grades.
appearance_dry: Tight, fine, slender strands with a dark glossy colour.
appearance_wet: As is typical of the class, soft even coppery-red leaf.
taste_profile: A fresh, lasting fragrance with clear sweetness, over a full red cup.

brewing.notes: Treat it like a Keemun: a porcelain gaiwan, hot water and short steeps will show the aroma best.

vintage_note: Usually sold as recent-harvest tea, with no special ageing culture on record. As with other gongfu blacks, the aroma is at its best in the first year or two. Fuliang's geographical label also covers green tea, so check that you are buying the black.
description:
Fu Hong is the gongfu black tea of Fuliang, the county around Jingdezhen in northeast Jiangxi, mostly grown in its north and northeast. Yes, the porcelain city: Fuliang is its tea-growing neighbourhood, and its tea carries a protected agricultural label.

It is made in the usual gongfu way, by withering, rolling, oxidising and drying, then sorted into fine strands. Some writing lumps it together with Keemun (qi hong), so the two names are easy to confuse. Whether a given bag is a separate style or a neighbour selling on a famous name is worth asking.

The cup is a deep red with a fresh, lingering sweet fragrance. Short steeps in porcelain suit it, and it is gentle enough to try against a Keemun side by side, which is the most useful way to learn what it is.

Fuliang also makes green tea under the same county label, so check the type before you buy. Ask for the harvest year and the grower's area.
history:
Fuliang's fame as a tea market is older than black tea itself: Bai Juyi's Tang-dynasty poem Pipa Xing mentions a merchant going to Fuliang to buy tea. That says nothing about this particular style, which came much later.

Local accounts credit Fuliang gongfu black tea with a gold award at the 1915 Panama-Pacific exposition, a claim made for several Chinese teas. Today Fuliang tea is a national agricultural geographical indication.
